shared_context.content: For each integer m >= 0, define F_m on sign sequences of length m-1 (and on the empty sequence when m=0 or m=1) by: F_m(t) is the number of permutations a=(a_1,...,a_m) of {1,...,m} such that t_i (a_{i+1}-a_i) > 0 for every admissible i. Set F_0(empty)=1 and F_1(empty)=1.
shared_context.label: Permutation-count function F_m

shared_context.content: If t=(t_1,...,t_{m-1}) with each t_i in {+1,-1}, define Peak(t) subseteq {1,...,m} by: 1 is in Peak(t) iff t_1=-1; m is in Peak(t) iff t_{m-1}=+1; and for 2 <= p <= m-1, p is in Peak(t) iff t_{p-1}=+1 and t_p=-1.
shared_context.label: Peak set of a sign sequence

shared_context.content: For m >= 1, let alt_m^+ be the sign sequence of length m-1 with entries +1,-1,+1,-1,..., so alt_m^+(i)=+1 for odd i and alt_m^+(i)=-1 for even i. Let alt_m^-=-alt_m^+, i.e. -1,+1,-1,+1,....
shared_context.label: Alternating sign sequences

shared_context.label: Alternating counts and Euler weights

strategy_summary: Strong induction on n using the position of the maximum entry. A recurrence expresses the count for an arbitrary sign pattern as a sum over the positions where the value n can occur. After replacing the smaller factors by the corresponding alternating-pattern maxima, the problem becomes a weighted independent-set problem on the path {1,...,n}. A bottleneck lemma says those Euler-type weights are maximized exactly by one full parity class of vertices, and those parity classes correspond exactly to the two alternating sign sequences.
